'''John Vincent Pardon''' (born June 1989) is an American mathematician who works on [[geometry]] and [[topology]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.claymath.org/people/john-pardon/|title=John Pardon|access-date=July 24, 2026|archive-date=July 24, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260724054554/https://www.claymath.org/people/john-pardon/|url-status=live}}</ref> He is primarily known for having solved [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Gromov]]'s problem on [[stretch factor|distortion]] of knots, for which he received the 2012 [[Morgan Prize]]. He is a permanent member of the [[Simons Center for Geometry and Physics]] in [[Stony Brook, New York]]. He was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] in 2026.<ref name="auto">{{cite web | title=Fields Medals 2026 | website=www.mathunion.org | url=https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/fields-medal/fields-medals-2026 | access-date=July 23, 2026 | archive-date=July 23, 2026 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260723135714/https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/fields-medal/fields-medals-2026 | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Early life==
Pardon's mother, Joyce Eileen Maggio Pardon, was a math teacher. She introduced him to basic arithmetic, trigonometry, and calculus. His father, William Pardon, was a mathematics professor at [[Duke University]].<ref name="eq"/>

Pardon was a three-time gold medalist at the [[International Olympiad in Informatics]], in 2005, 2006, and 2007.<ref>{{citation|url=http://stats.ioinformatics.org/halloffame/|title=Hall of Fame|work=International Olympiad in Informatics|accessdate=November 26, 2015|archive-date=August 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150816090851/http://stats.ioinformatics.org/halloffame/|url-status=live}}.</ref> In 2007, he placed second in the [[Intel Science Talent Search]] competition, with a generalization to [[rectifiable curve]]s of the [[carpenter's rule problem]] for polygons. In the project, he showed that every rectifiable [[Jordan curve]] in the plane can be continuously deformed into a [[convex curve]] without changing its length and without ever allowing any two points of the curve to get closer to each other.<ref>Aimee Cunningham, "The Next Generation", ''[[Science News]]'', March 17, 2007, p. 166.</ref> He published this research in the ''[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]]'' in 2009.

After high school, Pardon attended [[Princeton University]], where, after his sophomore year, he began taking graduate-level mathematics classes.<ref name="eq" /> As a student there, he solved a problem in [[knot theory]] posed by [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Mikhail Gromov]] in 1983 about whether every [[Knot (mathematics)|knot]] can be [[Embedding|embedded]] into three-dimensional space with bounded [[stretch factor]]. He showed that on the contrary, the stretch factor of certain [[torus knot]]s could be arbitrarily large.
His proof was published in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'' in 2011, and it earned him the [[Morgan Prize]] of 2012.<ref name="eq" /><ref name=clay>{{citation |url=http://www.claymath.org/events/news/research-fellow-john-pardon |title=Research Fellow: John Pardon |date=January 28, 2015 |publisher=[[Clay Mathematics Institute]] |accessdate=November 27, 2015 |archive-date=September 22, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220922003608/http://www.claymath.org/events/news/research-fellow-john-pardon |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{citation|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201204/rtx120400569p.pdf|title=2012 Morgan Prize|date=April 2012|pages=569–571|volume=59|issue=4|first=Elaine|last=Kehoe|access-date=April 28, 2021|archive-date=January 26, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250126054350/http://www.ams.org/notices/201204/rtx120400569p.pdf|url-status=live}}.</ref> 

In college, Pardon became fluent in Chinese.<ref name=":0" /> He later recalled, "I was signing up for classes as a freshman in college, and I heard Chinese was pretty difficult, so I wanted a challenge."<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=2026-07-23 |title=John Pardon Untangles the Theoretical Loops |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/23/science/john-pardon-fields-medal.html |access-date=2026-07-26 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He participated in a Chinese-language immersion program at Princeton and represented the university in an international debate competition in [[Singapore]], broadcast on Chinese television. As a [[cello]] player, he was a two-time winner of the Princeton Sinfonia concerto competition. He graduated in 2011 and was the [[valedictorian]] of his class.<ref name="eq">{{citation |url=https://www.princeton.edu/main/news/archive/S30/58/27Q66/index.xml |title=Pardon breaks new ground on path to becoming valedictorian |date=May 23, 2011 |first=Eric |last=Quiñones |work=News at Princeton |publisher=[[Princeton University]] |accessdate=November 26, 2015 |archive-date=May 17, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170517211453/http://www.princeton.edu/main/news/archive/S30/58/27Q66/index.xml |url-status=live }}.</ref> He then went to [[Stanford University]] for his graduate studies. His accomplishments there included solving the three-dimensional case of the [[Hilbert–Smith conjecture]]. He completed his Ph.D. in 2015, under the supervision of [[Yakov Eliashberg]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=196713}}</ref> In 2015, he was also appointed to a five-year term as a [[Clay Mathematics Institute|Clay Research Fellow]].<ref name=clay/>

== Career ==
Starting in 2015, Pardon served a yearlong appointment as an assistant professor at Stanford University. In the fall of 2016, he became a full professor of [[Mathematics]] at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.princeton.edu/main/news/archive/S46/12/66C86/index.xml?section=topstories|title=Board approves two faculty appointments|access-date=August 14, 2016|archive-date=August 22, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822045437/https://www.princeton.edu/main/news/archive/S46/12/66C86/index.xml?section=topstories|url-status=live}}</ref> He is currently a permanent member of the [[Simons Center for Geometry and Physics]] in [[Stony Brook, New York]]. In 2023, he proved the [[Maulik–Nekrasov–Okounkov–Pandharipande conjecture|Maulik–Nekrasov–Okounkov–Pandharipande (MNOP) conjecture]],<ref>{{cite arXiv | last=Pardon | first=John | title=Universally counting curves in Calabi--Yau threefolds | date=2023 | class=math.AG | eprint=2308.02948 }}</ref> which posited an equivalence between two different curve enumeration invariants of [[Calabi-Yau manifold|Calabi–Yau threefolds]]. He is currently working on a book about the foundations of [[symplectic geometry]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |last1=Kakaes |first1=Konstantin |title=The Quietest Mathematician Has Always Been Worth Listening To |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/john-pardon-wins-the-2026-fields-medal-for-work-in-symplectic-geometry-20260723/ |publisher=Quanta Magazine |access-date=24 July 2026 |language=en |date=23 July 2026 |archive-date=July 24, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260724060440/https://www.quantamagazine.org/john-pardon-wins-the-2026-fields-medal-for-work-in-symplectic-geometry-20260723 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 2017, Pardon received the [[National Science Foundation]]'s [[Alan T. Waterman Award]] for his contributions to geometry and topology.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.princeton.edu/news/home-page/professor-john-pardon-11-receives-nsf-waterman-award |title=Professor John Pardon '11 Receives NSF Waterman Award {{!}} Department of Mathematics |website=www.math.princeton.edu |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170414163450/http://www.math.princeton.edu/news/home-page/professor-john-pardon-11-receives-nsf-waterman-award |archive-date=April 14, 2017}}</ref>

He was elected to the 2018 class of [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://ams.org/profession/ams-fellows/new-fellows|title=2018 Class of the Fellows of the AMS|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|accessdate=November 3, 2017|archive-date=May 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190516101122/http://ams.org/profession/ams-fellows/new-fellows|url-status=live}}</ref> Also in 2018 he was an [[List of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers#2018, Rio de Janeiro|invited speaker]] at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] (ICM) in [[Rio de Janeiro]]. In 2022 he was awarded the [[Clay Research Award]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.claymath.org/news/2022-clay-research-award/|title=2022 Clay Research Award|access-date=July 24, 2026|archive-date=July 10, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260710122431/https://www.claymath.org/news/2022-clay-research-award/|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2025, he was awarded the [[Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics#New Horizons in Mathematics Prize|New Horizons in Mathematics Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 5, 2025 |title=Breakthrough Prize Announces 2025 Laureates in Life Sciences, Fundamental Physics, and Mathematics. |url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/91 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250406015731/https%3A%2F%2Fbreakthroughprize.org%2FNews%2F91 |archive-date=April 6, 2025 |access-date=April 6, 2025 |website=News |publisher=Breakthrough Prize}}</ref>

Pardon was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] at ICM Philadelphia 2026 for "achievements in symplectic geometry including new approaches to virtual fundamental cycles, Fukaya categories of certain manifolds and counting holomorphic curves, and for his contributions to other areas of geometry and topology, including group actions on 3-manifolds and knot theory".<ref name="auto"/>

== Personal life ==
Pardon has two sons, Alexandros and Andreas. In the Fields Medal award video produced by the [[Simons Foundation]], Pardon said he quizzes them in Chinese: "I talk to them in Chinese a lot. We learn the characters. I read to them. I make them read to me."<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E4KP07YL0Js |title=2026 Fields Medal: John Pardon |date=2026-07-23 |last=Simons Foundation |access-date=2026-08-10 |via=YouTube}}</ref>
His sister, Professor Mireille J. Pardon, is a noted medieval historian with a large TikTok following.<ref>2023 A.W. Mellon Junior Faculty Fellowship in Medieval Studies, Medieval Institute, Notre Dame. https://medieval.nd.edu/news-events/annual-events/mellon-colloquium/</ref>
<ref>Academia.edu CV https://berea.academia.edu/MireillePardon/CurriculumVitae</ref>
<ref>Berea College https://www.berea.edu/facultyMember/dr-mireille-j-pardon</ref>
<ref>https://www.tiktok.com/@pardon_mi</ref>
